687.title: Guru Hargobind's gurpurab
687.hook: remembered with the two swords of miri and piri
687.howItsDone: On Guru Hargobind's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some communities display gatka; Sikhs remember his two swords of miri and piri and the Akal Takht he founded.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baoli, and your line: eighty-four steps. Did you take one rushed task slowly, step by step? We skip ahead today, past the fifth Guru, to his son. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

A boy, about eleven by tradition's count, has just lost his father. Not to an accident. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the man who built the Harmandir Sahib and gathered the Granth, has died in custody in Lahore; Sikhs remember it as his shaheedi, his martyrdom. The Sikhs are grieving and afraid. And when the boy becomes the sixth Guru, he does something new. Tradition says he asks for two swords, and he puts on both. Today: Akal Takht.
screen: `A BOY WHO HAS LOST HIS FATHER.` → `A MARTYRDOM IN LAHORE.` → `HE PUTS ON TWO SWORDS.`

segments.voice: Guru Hargobind was born near Amritsar. You've met his birth already: the shabad of Guru Arjan's joy when his son arrived. After his father's execution, he became Guru, and the two swords he wore became a lasting idea in Sikh life. One sword was miri: worldly power, responsibility in the world, the duty to protect. The other was piri: spiritual authority, the life of devotion and the Name. Miri and piri. The words echo two titles: mir, a ruler, and pir, a spiritual guide. The point wasn't two separate lives. It was that a Sikh holds both at once. As Sikhs often explain it, devotion without courage can abandon the weak, and power without devotion turns cruel. The two swords keep each other honest. He gave the idea a building. Facing the Harmandir Sahib, he raised a platform called the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One. The Harmandir is where the Word is sung. The Akal Takht is where the community gathers to decide, and act. Even today, they stand looking at each other across the same courtyard. Guru Hargobind kept horses and armed followers, and fought battles with Mughal forces. He was also, tradition remembers, a man of deep devotion who kept the kirtan going morning and evening. The two outer swords of the Khanda emblem are often read the same way. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan, and in some places with displays of gatka, the Sikh martial art. Two swords, one Guru.
screen: `AFTER HIS FATHER'S EXECUTION.` · `MIRI AND PIRI: TWO SWORDS.` · `EACH KEEPS THE OTHER HONEST.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT FACES THE HARMANDIR.` · then, large: `TWO SWORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand tall. If you can, stand up. Feet planted, shoulders back, chin level. Feel your weight evenly on both feet: one side for your duties in the world, one for your inner life. Notice if you lean more on one. Gently even them out. Breathe in strength, breathe out stillness. If you can't stand, sit as tall as you can. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing like that. The bell holds the time.
Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One Guru Hargobind raised facing the Harmandir Sahib, where the community gathers to decide and act.
Your line: two swords. Today, notice one place where you need more courage, and one where you need more devotion, and give a little to each. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

what it means: they hold duty in the world and devotion to God together.

688.title: Guru Har Rai's gurpurab
688.howItsDone: On Guru Har Rai's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some Sikhs mark it by planting trees, tending gardens or serving in health care, remembering the seventh Guru's gardens and medicine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akal Takht, and your line: two swords. Did you give a little courage and a little devotion where each was needed? Today, his grandson, who kept the swords and was remembered for flowers. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Sikhs tell a story about a boy walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe. As he passes, the hem of the robe catches a flower and snaps its stem. The petals fall. His grandfather sees it and says something gentle: if you wear a robe like that, you have to carry it carefully. The boy is said to have held his robe gathered close for the rest of his life, so it would never break a flower again. That boy became the seventh Guru. Today: Har Rai.
screen: `A ROBE CATCHES A FLOWER.` → `THE GRANDFATHER'S GENTLE WORD.` → `A ROBE HELD CLOSE FOR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Rai was the grandson of Guru Hargobind, and he succeeded him as the seventh Guru while still young. He made his home at Kiratpur, in the hills of Punjab. The story of the flower is tradition, not a record, but it fits how Sikhs remember him: a gentle man, careful with living things. At Kiratpur, he's remembered for gardens: fruit trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs. Tradition says he kept a dispensary there, where medicines were made and given freely to anyone who came. He also kept the armed horsemen his grandfather had begun, but his years as Guru were largely peaceful. One story about his medicine reaches all the way to the Mughal court. Tradition tells that Dara Shikoh, a son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell gravely ill, and the court's physicians couldn't find a remedy. A rare herb was needed, and it was sent from Guru Har Rai's stores. Dara recovered. The striking part is who got the medicine: a prince of the same ruling house that had executed the Guru's great-grandfather, Guru Arjan. The healer didn't ask which side the patient was on. Sikh tradition reads that as the teaching heard all through the Gurus' hymns: the One is in everyone, so care goes to everyone. His gurpurab is marked with kirtan and langar, and some gurdwaras and families mark it with things he'd recognize: planting trees, tending gardens, or volunteering in clinics. The healer, remembered by healing.
screen: `A GENTLE GURU AT KIRATPUR.` · `GARDENS AND A DISPENSARY.` · `MEDICINE FOR THE EMPEROR'S SON.` · `CARE FOR EVERYONE, NO SIDES.` · then, large: `THE HEALER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: water a plant. If there's a plant near you, bring it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil darken. If there isn't, picture one you love, or a tree you pass each day. As you water, think of one living thing you could be more careful with: a person, an animal, a place. Gather your robe, so to speak. If you pray, Waheguru can go in with the water. The bell holds the time.
Har Rai, the seventh Guru, remembered on his gurpurab with gardens, herbs, and medicine given freely, even to the emperor's son.
Your line: the healer. Today, do one small act of care for something living, and do it without asking whose side it's on. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab
689.hook: remembered with care for the sick at Bangla Sahib
689.howItsDone: On Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab, Sikhs gather at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and elsewhere for kirtan and langar; many take water from Bangla Sahib's pool to the sick and serve the unwell in his memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Har Rai, and your line: the healer. Did you care for one living thing without asking whose side it was on? Today, his son, the youngest of all the Gurus. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

In the middle of New Delhi, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool. Day and night, people come with bottles to take its water home to someone sick. Its langar hall serves meals from morning to night. And the whole place is built around the memory of a child, who came to Delhi because an emperor summoned him, and stayed to look after the sick. Today: Bangla Sahib.
screen: `A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.` → `BOTTLES OF WATER FOR THE SICK.` → `THE MEMORY OF A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Krishan was the younger son of Guru Har Rai. Before his father died, he named the boy as the eighth Guru; tradition says he was about five. Some objected, including his older brother, Ram Rai, who had gone to the Mughal court and won favor there. The emperor Aurangzeb summoned the young Guru to Delhi. In Delhi, he stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh, a Rajput noble. That house is now Gurdwara Bangla Sahib: bangla means bungalow. While he was there, an epidemic struck the city; tradition usually names smallpox, and some accounts say cholera. Tradition says the child Guru went out among the sick, of every faith, giving water and comfort and care. He caught the disease himself and died, still a child; tradition says he was about eight. Tradition says his last words, when asked who would follow him, were Baba Bakale: the next Guru is at Bakala, which proved to be Guru Tegh Bahadur. The Sikh Ardas, which you learned line by line this year, remembers him in a single line. In paraphrase: remember Guru Har Krishan, at the sight of whom all suffering departs. Today, the pool at Bangla Sahib is where people take water for the sick, in his memory. His gurpurab is marked there with kirtan and with the langar, and some Sikhs visit or serve the sick that day. A very short life, remembered for care that walked toward the sickness instead of away from it.
screen: `THE EIGHTH GURU, AT FIVE.` · `A BUNGALOW IN DELHI.` · `AMONG THE SICK, AND STRICKEN.` · `REMEMBERED IN THE ARDAS.` · then, large: `THE CHILD HEALER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone unwell. Sit, and bring to mind one person you know who's sick, recovering or worn out. Picture them clearly. Then think of one small, real thing that would help: a message, a meal, a ride, an errand, an hour of company. Decide when you'll do it. Hold them in your mind with care until the bell. If you pray, you can say the Ardas line for them in your own way, or just Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Bangla Sahib, the Delhi gurdwara built around the bungalow where the child Guru stayed and cared for the sick in an epidemic.
Your line: the child healer. Today, do the one small thing you chose for someone who's unwell. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: The first installation
690.hook: the day the Adi Granth was first placed in the Harmandir in 1604 is celebrated in late summer
690.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate the Pehla Prakash, the first installation of the Adi Granth in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604, with kirtan, illuminations and a procession at Amritsar, and with special programs in gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bangla Sahib, and your line: the child healer. Did you do one small thing for someone unwell? We've walked through the Gurus' days. Now, two days for the book itself. Day six hundred ninety.

A passport. A house deed. A letter from someone who's gone. Nobody tosses papers like that into a bag; they get carried with two hands. In 1604, Sikhs carried a book that way: the words of the Gurus and saints, gathered over years and copied by hand, brought for the first time into the building raised to house it. Who carried it? Where did it sit? And where did the Guru sit? Today: Adi Granth.
screen: `HELD WITH TWO HANDS.` → `A BOOK COPIED BY HAND.` → `CARRIED IN FOR THE FIRST TIME.`

segments.voice: By the early 1600s, Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, had gathered the hymns of the first five Gurus, along with those of Hindu and Muslim saints whose words shared the Gurus' vision. Bhai Gurdas wrote them out as scribe. The finished volume was called the Adi Granth, the first book. In 1604, it was carried into the newly built Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar and opened there for the first time. Sikh tradition remembers the scene. Baba Buddha, a revered elder who had known Guru Nanak himself, carried the Granth on his head. He was appointed its first granthi, the one who reads it and cares for it. The Granth was placed on a raised seat, and Guru Arjan sat below it. The Guru, at a lower level than the book. That small detail says a great deal about what was coming. Then the Granth was opened at random, as it still is each day, for the first hukamnama, the day's command. Tradition gives the first one as a shabad of Guru Arjan in Raag Suhi, on Ang seven eighty-three. In paraphrase: the Lord Himself stood up to complete the work of His saints; the Lord came to do the work. Sikhs mark this day as the Pehla Prakash, the first opening, in late summer. At the Harmandir Sahib it's celebrated with kirtan, lights and a great procession. And every morning since, in that same building, the Granth has been carried in and opened again: the word, installed.
screen: `GURU ARJAN GATHERS THE ADI GRANTH.` · `BABA BUDDHA CARRIES IT IN.` · `THE GURU SITS BELOW THE BOOK.` · `THE FIRST HUKAMNAMA.` · then, large: `THE WORD INSTALLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a book reverently. Take any book that matters to you: a scripture, a gutka, a book of poems, a book someone gave you. Hold it with both hands. Before you open it, pause. Then open it slowly, wherever it falls, and read just one line, as if it were addressed to you today. Sit with that line until the bell. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before you open it. The bell holds the time.
Adi Granth, the first book of the Gurus' hymns, carried into the Harmandir Sahib in 1604 by Baba Buddha, with Guru Arjan seated below it.
Your line: the word installed. Today, give one book or one set of words a place of honor where you live, even a small one. Day six hundred ninety.

691.title: Guruship to the Granth
691.hook: the day in 1708 the Guru Granth Sahib became Guru is marked each autumn
691.howItsDone: Sikhs mark Gurta Gaddi Divas each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded, where Guru Gobind Singh conferred guruship on the Granth in 1708.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adi Granth, and your line: the word installed. Did you give one book a place of honor? A hundred and four years after that first opening, the book received something more than a place. Day six hundred ninety-one.

A community led by a living teacher meets a hard question sooner or later: what happens after? Who guides it when the teacher is gone? For the Sikhs, that question came to a head in 1708, far from Punjab, at Nanded in the Deccan, by the Godavari river. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, had been gravely wounded. His four sons had all died before him. The Sikhs around him asked who would guide them next. Today: Gurta Gaddi.
screen: `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER?` → `NANDED, 1708.` → `WHO WILL GUIDE US NEXT?`

segments.voice: Gurta Gaddi means the throne of guruship: gaddi is the seat, the cushion of authority, and gurta is the office of the Guru. Sikh tradition remembers what happened at Nanded in 1708. Guru Gobind Singh placed five coins and a coconut before the Granth, the same sign used when one Guru installed the next, and bowed to it. He declared that after him there would be no human Guru. The Granth itself, now called the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the Guru. For Sikhs, not only a holy book, but the Guru, living in the Word. Tradition says that not long before, at Damdama Sahib, the Granth had been completed with the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. So the Word was whole. Sikhs also speak of the Guru Panth, the community of the Khalsa, as carrying the Guru's authority together, guided by the Granth. And after the Ardas, sangats often sing a couplet that says: by the command of the Timeless One the Panth was established; all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as Guru. That couplet comes from later Sikh writings rather than the Granth itself, but it puts the teaching in a line sangats sing together. What follows is simple and large. In Sikh understanding, every Sikh, anywhere in the world, has direct access to the Guru. No human successor standing between a Sikh and the Guru. Just the Word, opened each morning, read each night. The Gurta Gaddi Divas is marked each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Hazur Sahib in Nanded.
screen: `GURTA GADDI: THE THRONE OF GURUSHIP.` · `NANDED: FIVE COINS AND A COCONUT.` · `THE WORD, COMPLETE AT DAMDAMA.` · `THE GURU IN EVERY SIKH'S REACH.` · then, large: `THE ETERNAL GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow to the Granth. If there's a Guru Granth Sahib or a gutka near you, go to it, and bow, the way Sikhs do on entering the darbar. If there isn't, picture one: the Granth on its raised seat, covered in cloth, a granthi waving the chaur above it. Bow your head toward that picture, slowly. Let the bow mean: I'm ready to listen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you rise. The bell holds the time.
Gurta Gaddi. The throne of guruship, given by Guru Gobind Singh to the Granth at Nanded in 1708: from then on, Sikhs revere the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.
Your line: the eternal guru. Today, when you need guidance, open a page of words you trust before you open your phone. Day six hundred ninety-one.

screen: `DAY 691 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING BACK: THE DAILY BANIS.`

692.title: Looking back: the daily banis
692.hook: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, heard in order
692.howItsDone: Many Sikhs say the Japji, Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye in the early morning, often with Chaupai and Anand Sahib, then Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurta Gaddi: in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and your line, the eternal guru. Did you bow, or simply pause, before a book of the Guru's words? Today we turn around and look back at the year. Day six hundred ninety-two.

Six banis. One day. A Sikh home before dawn: a kettle, a dark window, a voice already reading. By breakfast, several prayers have passed. At dusk, another. At bedtime, one more, said with the lights low. This year you met each of those prayers on its own, block by block, sometimes for weeks at a time. Today, for once, you hear them the way they're actually lived: in order, one day long. Looking back: the daily banis.
screen: `SIX BANIS, ONE DAY.` → `MORNING, DUSK, NIGHT.` → `HEARD IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Start in the dark. Amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, is when the Sikh code of conduct asks a Sikh to rise, bathe and begin. After the Japji comes the Jaap Sahib, which Sikhs know as Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise, all short lines and quick meters. You met its line in the spring: namastvam akaale, salutation to the One beyond time. Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, ten verses under the heading by Your grace. The poet has seen monks, yogis and mighty kings by the thousand, and says all of it is worth nothing without love. Then, in some homes, the Benti Chaupai, a prayer for shelter: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, give me Your hand and keep me safe. And then Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, which opens with a cry of joy: anand bhaiaa meree maae, I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the morning. Then comes the day itself: work, traffic, dishes, people. The banis don't ask anyone to leave it. They frame it. At dusk, as work ends, Rehras, the evening prayer. It opens with So Dar, the door where the Creator sits and cares for all. And last, at bedtime, Kirtan Sohila, five short hymns, beginning jai ghar keerat aakheeai: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung. The same hymns are sung at funerals, so the close of a day and the close of a life share one song. Notice what the order does. Praise first, before anything has happened. Shelter for the hours ahead. Joy. A door at dusk. A song for sleep. The whole day, held between words.
screen: `AMRITVELA: JAAP AND THE SAVAIYE.` · `SHELTER AND BLISS: CHAUPAI, ANAND.` · `DUSK: REHRAS, AS WORK ENDS.` · `NIGHT: SOHILA, THE SONG FOR SLEEP.` · then, large: `THE DAY, HELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line from each, six lines, one day. Sit comfortably. Say them slowly, aloud or under your breath, with a full breath between each. Namastvam akaale. Tav prasad, by Your grace. Hamree karo hath dai rachhaa. Anand bhaiaa meree maae. So dar. Jai ghar keerat aakheeai. If a line won't come, say it in English, and let that be enough. Then rest in the quiet that's left after the sixth. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Turning around near the top of the year to see the daily banis together: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, from before dawn to bedtime.
Your line: the day, held. Today, notice the two edges of your day, the first thing you do and the last, and give one of them a line. Day six hundred ninety-two.

screen: `DAY 692 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING BACK: THE LONG HYMNS.`

693.title: Looking back: the long hymns
693.hook: Sukhmani, Asa di Var, Barah Maha and the ninth Guru's saloks
693.howItsDone: Many Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily or in family gatherings, gurdwaras sing Asa di Var before sunrise, the Barah Maha is read on Sangrand, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of a full reading of the Granth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the daily banis, Jaap at dawn to Sohila at night, and your line, the day, held. Which edge of your day got a line? Today, the long hymns. Day six hundred ninety-three.

Some prayers fit in a breath. Others take an hour and more, and people make room for them anyway. In some Sikh families, when someone is ill or a home is starting something new, relatives gather on the floor to read Sukhmani Sahib together, start to finish, passing the reading along. In gurdwaras before sunrise, ragis are already singing a ballad that will run until the sky goes pale. Long hymns ask for something short ones don't: time, and often company. This year gave you four of them. Looking back: the long hymns.
screen: `SOME PRAYERS FIT IN A BREATH.` → `SOME TAKE AN HOUR, TOGETHER.` → `FOUR LONG HYMNS.`

segments.voice: First, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's psalm of peace, in Raga Gauri. Twenty-four ashtpadis, each opening with a salok and then eight stanzas. Some read it whole; some read a part each day. Its refrain names the whole hymn: sukhmani sukh amrit prabh naam, the jewel of peace is God's ambrosial Name, the resting place of the devotees' minds. We spent a hundred days on it, longer than on anything else this year. Second, Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's ballad for dawn. A var was a hero's ballad, the kind sung about kings and battles. Guru Nanak took the form and turned it inward: twenty-four pauris, with saloks of Guru Nanak and Guru Angad, and in the gurdwara Guru Ram Das's chhants sung between them. Its first salok is gratitude: balihaaree gur aapne, a sacrifice to my Guru, a hundred times a day. Third, the Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's twelve months in Raga Majh. In the old Punjabi form, a woman longs for her absent beloved as the seasons turn; here the longing is the soul's, for God. It opens with people separated by their own deeds, asking in mercy to be united, and Sikhs read it in gurdwaras on Sangrand, the first day of each month. Fourth, the saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, near the very end of the Granth. Short, calm couplets about a world that passes and a Name that stays. One says the wise person frightens no one and fears no one. Four long hymns, four moods: peace, gratitude, longing, steadiness. And this week has been a look back of its own: the Gurus' gurpurabs, the first installation, the Granth made Guru, and the daily banis.
screen: `SUKHMANI: THE JEWEL OF PEACE.` · `ASA DI VAR: A BALLAD AT DAWN.` · `BARAH MAHA: TWELVE MONTHS OF LONGING.` · `THE NINTH GURU'S STEADY SALOKS.` · then, large: `THE LONG HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one favorite. Peace, gratitude, longing or steadiness: pick the one you need today. Find a few lines of it in a gutka, a gurbani app, or simply in memory, and read them slowly, twice. Don't try to finish anything. Then sit with what you read for the rest of the time, letting one phrase come back now and then, like a tune you can't shake. If you pray, you can let those lines carry your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Four long hymns side by side: Sukhmani's peace, Asa di Var's gratitude, the Barah Maha's longing, and the ninth Guru's steady saloks.
Your line: the long hymns. Today, give one thing more time than it strictly needs: a meal, a phone call, a page. Day six hundred ninety-three. Another week, done.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak. a var is a ballad sung about kings and battles. what do you do with the form?
options: use it for the inner life and praise of God.
write a ballad about a famous battle.
fork.reveal: Asa di Var keeps the ballad's shape, twenty-four pauris, but its battles are inward, and it opens in gratitude to the Guru.

original.note: Punjabi: the jewel of peace, the name of Guru Arjan's long hymn in Raga Gauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: long hymns are for experts with hours to spare.
what it means: Sikhs read them a little a day, or together, so the length is shared.

what a scholar hears: both Sukhmani's twenty-four ashtpadis and Asa di Var's twenty-four pauris are numbered structures, and tradition holds that the ninth Guru's saloks were added when the Granth was completed at Damdama.
